the-mouth of the Piscataquis River in Kitteiy Point. We appreciate the efforts of the Friends of .

rich history.
Although there is scant written information on Indigenous peoples` activities in the region,

Following colonial settlement, the site served intennittently for coastal defense in the late l7"` century. Fort McClary was officially established in 1808 and was named after Maj or Andrew McClaiy, an American officer killed in the 1775 Battle of Bunker Hill. The Fort was in operation throughout the 1800s and saw active use during the Civil War. In the early 1900s, the Foit fell into disrepair, and the state of Maine acquired the property from the federal govermneiit in 1924. The Fort was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1969.

Testimony of Eliza Townsend
in support of LD 1019
An Act to Provide Funding for Fort McClary
March 25, 2025
Good afternoon, Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker and distinguished members of
the ACF Committee, I am Eliza Townsend, Maine Conservation Policy Director for the
Appalachian Mountain Club.
AMC is a people-oriented conservation nonprofit; our mission is the protection, understanding, and enjoyment of the outdoors. We have 6,200 members in Maine and manage 130,000 acres
of forestland in Piscataquis County for multiple use, including sustainable forestry, backcountry
recreation, and outdoor education. We pay property taxes on all of our land.
We support LD 1019, which appropriates $60,000 in one-time funds for renovations and
maintenance to restore and preserve the Fort McClary State Historic Site in Kittery Point. Fort
McClary marks both U.S. military and commercial history. A fort was first constructed on the
site in 1690 in response to the imposition of a customs duty by the colony of New Hampshire. My favorite fact about Fort McClary, however, is that Hannibal Hamlin served there as cook to his U.S. Coast Guard Unit during the summer of 1864. He was the Vice President of the United
States at the time!
Along with memorializing the military use of this strategic location, Fort McClary State Historic Site offers close-to-home access to the outdoors. The site's dramatic view of the Piscataqua
River, fortifications and buildings to explore, picnic tables and relatively low entry fees make it a
wonderful destination for a family outing. In these harried times, such locations are invaluable.
Despite being managed by the Bureau of Parks and Lands and rounding out our public outdoor recreation offerings, the state's historic sites were ineligible to share in the $50 million
allocated by the 130"` legislature from the American Rescue Plan Act for investment in Maine's state parks. Like the state parks, the historic sites have long suffered from a lack of investment.
It is time to correct that neglect. For that reason, we support not only LD 1019 to invest in Fort McClary, but also the two bills sponsored by Senator Grohoski to invest a total of $18 million in
Maine's 15 historic sites, from Fort McClary at Kittery Point, to Fort Kent, on the banks of the Allagash River--and of course, our local favorite site, Katahdin Ironworks.
We urge you to vote LD 1019 Ought to Pass.

Testimony of Senator Mark W. Lawrence introducing
LD 1019, An Act to Provide Funding for Fort McClary
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry March 25, 2025

Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and Esteemed Members of the Joint Standing Committee
on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Mark Lawrence. I am the State Senator from
District 35 in southern York County, proudly representing Eliot, Kittery, Ogunquit, South Berwick and
York. I am here to present LD 1019, An Act to Provide Funding for Fort McClary.

For over 275 years, Fort McClary located in Kittery Point, has protected the approaches of the Piscataqua River, overlooking the southern entryway to Kittery and the Gulf of Maine. It stood ready to
defend important territory during the Revolutionary War, the War of 1812, the Civil War, the SpanishAmerican War and World War I. The site reminds the thousands of annual visitors about Maine's wartime history and how military architecture and teclmology has advanced over time.
Home to an aging brick magazine, rifleman's house and the landmark 1844 hexagonal blockhouse, the
remaining structures and land at Fort McClary served an important historical purpose through the five wars I mentioned previously. The Fort now serves another important purpose, teaching the next generation about that very history while serving as a first stop to thousands on their Maine vacations.
LD 1019 would provide $60,000 for renovations and maintenance to restore and preserve the Fort
McClary State Historic Site. Working in companionship with the Friends of Fort McClary, a group of
dedicated volunteers who plan park activities and raise funds to support the park, this appropriation will
go towards the renovations, maintenance needs and upkeep needed for the Fort to continue welcoming visitors from across the country and world.

The Maine Beaches Association reported that York County's economic tourism impact from direct visitor spending was approximately $2.3 billion in 2023. While the Fort isn't an economic driver itself, it's one of many attractions on visitor's lists and often followed by visits to our delicious local restaurants, unique small businesses or scenic lodging options. I firmly believe the investment proposed
in LD 1019 is a worthy one given the return on it we see countywide.

As you'll hear from supporters of LD 1019, this bill is more than just money for a fort. This bill aims to

preserve a relic of Maine and American history, one that's taught generations of Maine's unique

position in armed conflict. My constituents hold great pride in this site and what it means to our
community. As their senator, it brings me great pride to bring this legislation forward for your

consideration.

'

Thank you for the opportunity to present this bill, I would be happy to answer any questions the
Committee may have.
